transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Well, um... I guess what brought me in is I just don't feel like myself anymore. I barely talk to people these days. I just go flat and quiet. And work... even getting started on my cleaning route feels like pushing a loaded cart uphill. 

Literally, sometimes, because they bought these new utility carts for the building last month and the caster wheels on them are just terrible. They’re supposed to glide, but they catch on that thick industrial carpet on the third floor. I told Gary—he’s the night manager—I said, "Gary, these wheels are useless." He’s a good kid, actually. He reminds me of this guy I shared a dorm with when I took a couple semesters of college back in '84. Dave, I think his name was. We used to go to this 24-hour diner after studying that had the absolute best cherry pie. They closed it down a few years ago to build a bank, which is a real shame. Seems like every empty lot turns into a bank or a pharmacy now, you know? 

But, uh... I'm sorry, what was I saying? Right, why I'm here. Yeah, just... everything is a huge effort. I just don't have it in me to say much of anything to anyone lately.
Have you ever felt this way, or experienced a period like this, at any other time in your life before now?

Before now? Well... I mean, this current stretch, it’s been building for about a year and five months. Yeah, right around a year and five months, ever since I had to leave my old apartment and my old neighborhood. 

I really loved that neighborhood. I was on the second floor, right above this old hardware store. It was so convenient. If my sink leaked, I just walked downstairs and bought a washer for fifteen cents. The guy who ran it, Sal, he always had the baseball game playing on this dusty little radio. AM radio, you know, with that crackly static sound? It’s actually a really comforting sound. You don't hear much AM radio anymore. Everyone's got those little white pods shoved in their ears now. I see folks on my cleaning route doing it all the time. They don't even look up when I empty their office trash cans, just staring at their computer screens with those things in their ears. It’s rude, honestly. Back in the day, people at least nodded or said hello when you walked into a room. My dad always taught me to look a person in the eye when they enter a room. He was a mechanic, worked on transmissions mostly... 

But, um, what were you asking? Oh, if I felt like this before. I don't really know about before. I just know this whole thing started up after the move.
Since this started about a year and five months ago, have you noticed any changes in your physical health, or have you been diagnosed with any new medical conditions by a doctor?

Physical health? No, I haven't been to a doctor for anything new. I don't really go to the doctor much anyway, to be honest. Last time I went was... gosh, probably when I pulled a muscle in my back moving a couch. That was years ago, back when I lived in the old place. 

It was this heavy floral couch, the kind with the wooden trim along the bottom that weighs a ton. My buddy Craig helped me move it. Craig's a good guy, he works over at the post office on 4th Street. You know, the one with the really nice brickwork out front? They don't build post offices like that anymore. Now they're just these square concrete blocks, no character at all. It's like everything is just built to be cheap and fast. Same with the mops we get at work. The handles used to be solid wood, you could really get a grip on them. Now they're this hollow aluminum stuff that bends if you lean into a tough stain on the tile. And the mop heads? Don't even get me started on the mop heads. They unravel after two washes. I tried telling the supply guy, but he just shrugged. Nobody cares about quality anymore, it's all just... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Something about the doctor? Yeah, no, no new medical stuff. Just the same old me, I guess.
Have you ever felt like you were receiving special messages from things around you, or felt that people were watching you or talking about you in ways that others might not understand?

Well... yeah, actually. I do get these thoughts sometimes. Mostly about the new landlord and a couple of the people who live in my new building. I just... I get stuck on this idea that they're keeping tabs on me, you know? Like they're watching me through the hallway cameras and passing messages about me to each other. 

People tell me those cameras are just for the front door, just for security, but I don't know. The red light on them is always blinking. It reminds me of the blinking light on my old VCR. I held onto that thing for years because I had all these tapes of old boxing matches. Sugar Ray Leonard, Hagler, Hearns... the classics, you know? They don't fight like that anymore. Now it's all about who can talk the most trash on social media before the fight even happens. It's a spectacle, not a sport. My uncle used to box a little in the Navy. He was stationed out in San Diego in the late 60s. He brought me back this really cool model ship once, a destroyer. I kept it on my dresser until I was about twenty, then I think it got lost when I moved out of my parents' house...

But anyway, what was I saying? Right, the cameras. Yeah, I just can't shake the feeling they're using them to watch me and talk about me behind my back, even if everyone says I'm crazy for thinking it.
When you have these thoughts about the cameras and the neighbors, do you ever find that your own thoughts become jumbled or that you have trouble keeping your train of thought organized?

Yeah, I do. My thoughts get... well, they get really tangled up sometimes. Like, just the other day, my supervisor at work, he asked me a simple question. He just wanted to know which floors I had finished cleaning. And I tried to tell him, I really did, but then I started talking about the old bus route I used to take to get to the building. Route 42, the one that used to go past the community garden. 

I had a little plot there for a while, grew these amazing heirloom tomatoes. You can't buy tomatoes like that in the store, they taste like water. You gotta grow 'em yourself, get your hands in the dirt. My grandmother taught me that. She had this huge garden behind her house, right next to the church basement where they held the bingo nights. She'd win sometimes, too. She'd bring home these little plastic trinkets or maybe a five-dollar bill, and she was so proud of it. She always smelled like lavender and damp earth...

But, uh, where was I? Oh, right, my supervisor. Yeah, I was talking to him, and I could hear myself just going on about the church basement and the garden, and I realized I wasn't even answering his question about the floors. It's like my brain just takes a left turn and I can't steer it back.
Do you ever hear sounds, voices, or see things that other people around you do not seem to notice?

Well, yeah, sometimes I do. Mostly when I'm working late. When I'm mopping after hours, I'll hear a man's voice say my name, or tell me I've missed a spot. It sounds clear as day, like he's standing right by the stairwell. But when I look, there's nobody there. It's just me and the mop bucket. 

Those yellow mop buckets, you know the ones? The wheels always squeak on the left side. I tried oiling them once with some WD-40 I found in the supply closet, but it didn't do much good. WD-40 isn't really a lubricant anyway, it's a water displacer. My dad taught me that. He was a mechanic for forty years, worked on Fords mostly. He had this old Mustang he was restoring in the garage. Cherry red. He spent every weekend under the hood of that thing. He used to let me hold the flashlight for him, but if I didn't hold it exactly where he wanted, he'd get so frustrated. He had a short temper, my dad. Especially after he lost his hearing in one ear. He said it was from working around the engines all those years without ear protection. Nobody wore ear protection back then. It was just different times... 

But, uh, anyway. The voice. Yeah, I hear that guy by the stairwell, but nobody's ever there.
Aside from the times you feel quiet or flat, have you ever felt so low, sad, or hopeless that you felt like you couldn't get out of bed or stop crying for weeks at a time?

Yeah... yeah, I have. It's been like that a lot, actually. Ever since I moved into this new place, it's just been this heavy... this heavy feeling. Like I can't drag myself out from under it. For most of the time since the move, the sadness, the low energy... I just feel guilty about everything, and I don't care about the things I used to like. It's just been there in the background, you know? Even on the days when the voices in the stairwell or the worries about the hallway cameras are the main thing on my mind, that heavy sadness is still just sitting there. 

Moving is hard, though. I hired these movers, two young guys, and they broke my favorite lamp. It was this ugly brass thing, but my mom gave it to me when I got my first apartment. It had this fringed shade that gathered dust like crazy. I tried to fix it with superglue, but superglue never really holds brass together right, does it? You really need a proper weld for something like that. My dad could have fixed it. He had a welding torch in the garage, right next to where he kept the Mustang parts. He used to wear this big heavy welding mask, looked like Darth Vader or something. I went to see that movie in the theater when it came out, the first Star Wars. The line was wrapped all the way around the block. We stood out there for two hours in the heat, eating these stale pretzels from a street vendor... 

But, uh, what was I saying? Right, the sadness. Yeah, it's just been there almost every day since I moved, just making it hard to get out of bed.
